subject: anatomy
title: Gluteal region and hip joint: key anatomy for exams

steps.tx: The gluteal region is the gateway to the lower limb. The **greater sciatic foramen** is bounded by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments and is divided by the **piriformis** muscle. Structures above piriformis pass out with the superior gluteal nerve and vessels. Structures below it include the sciatic nerve, the inferior gluteal nerve and vessels, and the nerve to quadratus femoris.

steps.tx: The **lesser sciatic foramen** transmits the tendon of obturator internus, the pudendal nerve, the internal pudendal vessels and the nerve to obturator internus. Mnemonic PINTO. The inferior gluteal vessels do not pass through it, so they are the usual answer when this structure is asked about in MCQs.
steps.say: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the tendon of obturator internus, the pudendal nerve, the internal pudendal vessels and the nerve to obturator internus. The mnemonic is PINTO. The inferior gluteal vessels do not pass through it.

vis.alt: Posterior view of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina: the piriformis divides the greater foramen, with the superior gluteal nerve and vessels above it and the sciatic, inferior gluteal, pudendal and other nerves below it; the lesser foramen carries the obturator internus tendon, pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels and nerve to obturator internus.
vis.caption: Piriformis is the landmark: superior gluteal above, everything else below. The pudendal nerve leaves through the greater foramen and re-enters through the lesser.

steps.tx: The gluteal muscles and their nerves are high yield. **Superior gluteal nerve** (L4 to S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae. **Inferior gluteal nerve** (L5 to S2) supplies gluteus maximus alone. Injury to the superior gluteal nerve causes a positive Trendelenburg sign and a gluteal gait.

steps.tx: In a **positive Trendelenburg sign**, standing on one leg makes the pelvis drop on the opposite side, meaning the stance-side abductors are weak. Causes include superior gluteal nerve injury, hip dislocation, neck of femur fracture and greater trochanter fracture. Paralysis of gluteus maximus does not produce this sign.

Causes include superior gluteal nerve injury, hip dislocation, neck of femur fracture and greater trochanter fracture. Paralysis of gluteus maximus does not produce this sign.

vis.alt: Flow diagram of the Trendelenburg test: standing on the right leg needs right gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, to hold the pelvis level; if they fail the pelvis drops on the left, a positive sign.
vis.caption: The pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak stance-side abductors.

steps.tx: Blood supply to the **femoral head** comes mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery via its retinacular branches, especially the lateral retinacular artery. The obturator artery supplies a minor part through the artery of ligamentum teres. This is why a fracture of the femoral neck can cause avascular necrosis of the head.

vis.alt: Flow diagram of femoral head blood supply: medial circumflex femoral artery gives retinacular branches to the head as the main supply, lateral circumflex femoral is a lesser contributor, and the obturator artery gives the artery of the ligament of the head, minor in adults.
vis.caption: The medial circumflex femoral artery dominates; an intracapsular neck fracture can tear its retinacular branches and cause avascular necrosis.
